news.2026-11-22-basf-renonce-evonik.titl: BASF throws in the towel on Evonik: the target's shares suffer their worst session ever and end the week a quarter below the offer
news.2026-11-22-basf-renonce-evonik.summ: Chemicals group BASF has abandoned its bid to buy German rival Evonik, which had rejected two offers, the latest at 24 euros per share, or 11.2 billion euros. Evonik shares fell 16%, a record, then closed Friday at 18.18 euros after a downgrade by broker Oddo BHF [2][3][4].
news.2026-11-22-basf-renonce-evonik.poin: On Thursday, November 19, BASF announced it was ending its efforts to acquire Evonik Industries, after two non-binding, all-cash offers were rejected [2].

BASF faulted Evonik's management board for failing to “engage meaningfully,” even after signaling it could still raise its price [2][3]. According to BASF, Evonik's standalone prospects did not justify paying more [2].

The first offer, around 22.15 euros per share, valued Evonik at about 10.3 billion euros [8]. BASF had raised it to 24 euros, or 11.2 billion euros ($12.3 billion), with pledges to preserve jobs and sites [3][7].

Evonik shares plunged more than 23% at the low point of Thursday's session, according to Börsen-Zeitung [5][6], and closed with a record 16% drop, according to Reuters as cited by ad-hoc-news [4]. BASF shares edged higher [1][5].
On Friday, broker Oddo BHF cut its rating on Evonik to “neutral,” with a 19-euro price target. The stock closed at 18.18 euros (−0.7%), nearly a quarter below the 24 euros offered [4].

The RAG Foundation, Evonik's largest shareholder with about 44% of the capital, regretted that BASF pulled out without letting the two management teams hold more in-depth talks [3][9]. Political opposition to the deal was strong, and politicians have significant influence over the foundation [3].
BASF says acquisitions remain possible within its strategy but are not necessary for its growth [4].
Key takeaway: when a takeover offer disappears, the target's shares suddenly lose the “premium” investors had paid in the hope of receiving the offered price. Evonik thus wiped out in a single session much of what it had gained since BASF's interest was announced [4][5][12].

It was the biggest deal in BASF's history, presented as its answer to the crisis in the German chemicals industry [13]. BASF promised to protect Evonik's jobs and sites to win acceptance for the combination [7].
The failure shows the weight of “anchor” shareholders in Germany: with 44% of the capital, the RAG Foundation held the keys, and elected officials in the region weighed in [3][9].

For Börsen-Zeitung, the German financial daily, BASF's withdrawal is “a victory for reason”: the buyer avoids overpaying [5]. On Evonik's side, shareholders are left with a stock well below the offer they did not get [4].
news.2026-11-22-basf-renonce-evonik.forM: If you hold Evonik or a fund of German stocks, you have just seen the risk of “speculative” shares: buying in the hope of a takeover bid means betting on a deal that may never come. When the takeover falls through, the drop is brutal, often in a single session.

news.2026-11-22-basf-renonce-evonik.deep: How it works: the vanishing “takeover premium”

When a company announces it wants to buy another, it generally offers a price above the market price to persuade shareholders to sell. The target's shares then rise toward that price, without ever quite reaching it as long as the deal is not certain. Specialized investors even buy in to pocket the difference. If the buyer walks away, the whole bet collapses: they all sell at once and the stock falls back toward its “standalone” value, sometimes lower. Evonik, which BASF offered 24 euros [3], ended the week at 18.18 euros [4]. Conversely, the buyer often rises slightly, like BASF [1], because its shareholders feared it would overpay.
news.2026-11-22-basf-renonce-evonik.past: Precedents: three months of tug-of-war, and a takeover bid that succeeds elsewhere
BASF confirms exploratory talks with the RAG Foundation and Evonik, stating that their outcome remains open [10]. Evonik shares soar after the first reports of BASF's interest [12].
The takeover premium is priced into the stock from the first rumors, before any firm offer.
Evonik deems too low a first offer of about 22.15 euros per share, or 10.3 billion euros [8].
A rejection does not necessarily kill a takeover: BASF raised its price, which kept shareholders' hopes alive.
BASF raises its offer to 24 euros per share, 11.2 billion euros, with job guarantees, and is rejected a second time [3][7].
Even an improved offer fails without the support of the largest shareholder and elected officials.
In France, EP Group's takeover bid for Fnac Darty, at 35 euros per share, is reopened until November 25 inclusive [11].
When the buyer follows through, the stock stays anchored near the offered price: the exact opposite of Evonik.

news.2026-11-22-bitcoin-sous-57000-liqui: New York, United States
United States
Bitcoin loses nearly 10% in 24 hours and falls toward $55,000: more than $2 billion in bets liquidated over the weekend

On Saturday, November 21, the day after Wall Street entered correction territory, bitcoin plunged below $57,000, then toward $55,000, a drop of nearly 10% in 24 hours. Between $2.2 billion and $2.5 billion in leveraged bets were forcibly liquidated, according to specialized sites [1][2][3][4].

Bitcoin fell nearly 10% in 24 hours on Saturday and approached $55,000, according to KuCoin News and Bitcoin Foundation [1][4]. It was still worth $64,146 on the morning of November 18, according to Fortune [5].

Liquidations, the forced sales of positions bought on credit, exceeded $2.4 billion according to Bitcoinist [2], $2.38 billion according to The Defiant [3] and $2.5 billion according to KuCoin News [1].
Most of the losses, about $2.27 billion, hit investors who were betting on a rise [2][3].

Specialized sites cite three reasons: higher-than-expected US inflation, which revives fears of a Fed rate hike, outflows from bitcoin exchange-traded funds (ETFs), and the slump in AI-related stocks [2][4].
The drop extends that of the previous weekend: on November 14 and 15, bitcoin had already fallen to near $62,000, a four-month low, with about $2 billion in liquidations [6][7].

According to Decrypt, spot bitcoin ETFs had lost about $1.91 billion over seven straight sessions through November 13, and traders are now watching the $60,000 threshold, which has already been broken [6].
Safe-haven assets did not play their role this week: the selling wave also hit gold and silver, notes the site Marketcalls [8].

Key takeaway: bitcoin does not behave like a “digital gold” that protects in a storm, but like a risk asset that falls along with tech stocks. When Wall Street slides and rates may rise, it is among the first things sold [2][4][8].

Crypto trades 24 hours a day, 7 days a week. When stock exchanges are closed, it is one of the only markets where worried investors can sell. On weekends, trading is thinner, so each large sale weighs more heavily on the price [1][4].

The engine of the fall is leveraged bets. Billions of dollars had been wagered on a rise with borrowed money. When the price drops, platforms automatically sell these positions, which pushes the price down further and triggers more sales: a domino effect [2][3].
The link with the Fed is direct: higher rates make risk-free investments such as Treasury bills more attractive, and assets that pay no interest, such as bitcoin, less attractive [4].

If you have bought bitcoin or a product that tracks it, this weekend shows it can lose 10% while you sleep, even on a Saturday. And borrowing to invest multiplies losses: those who had bet on credit were forced to sell at the worst possible moment.

How it works: the “liquidation” of a leveraged bet

On cryptocurrency platforms, you can buy bitcoin with “leverage”: you put in $1,000, the platform lends you $9,000, and you trade on $10,000. If the price rises 10%, you double your stake. But if it falls about 10%, your stake is wiped out: the platform immediately sells the whole position to recover its loan. That is liquidation. When thousands of positions are sold at the same time, these automatic sales push the price down, which triggers further liquidations. On Saturday, about $2.27 billion in bets on a rise were blown up this way [2][3].

Belgium: the three main unions take to the streets in Brussels on Monday, as the De Wever government is still looking for 10 billion euros

This Monday, November 23, the CSC, FGTB and Synova are demonstrating together in Brussels against austerity and falling purchasing power. Metro, tram and bus services will be heavily disrupted. Prime Minister Bart De Wever, whose resignation the king refused in early November, still has no budget [1][2][3][5].
The three unions, united in a “common front,” denounce the federal government's austerity policy and the decline in purchasing power [3]. The call was issued as early as October 21 [7].

According to RTBF, the main march is due to set off at 10 a.m. from Brussels-North station, with a rally at Rogier at 11 a.m.; the CSC, for its part, announces an 11 a.m. start [2][4]. RTBF speaks of “thousands of demonstrators” expected, without a precise figure [2].
Brussels transport company STIB expects heavy disruption on the metro, tram and bus. The SNCB, meanwhile, reports no strike: trains should run normally [2].

The FGTB has filed a strike notice, and the CSC is promising compensation to members who lose wages by taking part [2][4]. L'Avenir also reports disruption in schools and speaks of an “11th action” [1].

In the background is the political crisis: Bart De Wever had tendered his resignation on November 2 after a failed meeting of his coalition. King Philippe refused it on November 6 and asked him to resume budget negotiations “immediately” [5][6].

At stake is an effort of 10 billion euros, combining spending cuts and new revenue [6]. Without an agreement, Bart De Wever has warned that 2027 would begin with an emergency budget that rolls over the previous year's [6].
Key takeaway: the street is putting pressure on a government that cannot finalize its budget, at the very moment it needs to find 10 billion euros in savings and revenue [3][6].

For Economie Matin, the king's refusal of the resignation reduced the short-term risk of new elections, but it guarantees neither the adoption of a budget nor calm on the markets, which are watching the cost of Belgian debt [6].

An emergency budget makes it possible to pay current expenses, but it blocks reforms and new measures. The longer the paralysis lasts, the greater the risk that Belgium drifts away from European fiscal rules.

The mobilization is part of a series of union actions since Bart De Wever's coalition took office, and it comes amid a wave of anger over the cost of living in several European countries, including France [1][3].

If you need to go through Brussels on Monday, allow plenty of time: STIB metro, trams and buses will be heavily disrupted, even if SNCB trains should run. More broadly, Belgium shows how hard it is to cut spending without a solid majority.

Military AI: Trump and Xi agree to leave decisions to humans, Washington says, but no text has been published

US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent says Donald Trump and Xi Jinping agreed in Shenzhen that military decisions made with artificial intelligence should remain under human control. Beijing speaks of AI that must remain “under human control,” but no detailed document exists [1][3].

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent announced it on CNBC after the APEC summit in Shenzhen: according to him, the two leaders agree that humans should take part in military decisions made with AI [1][2].

He sums up the idea this way: a “superintelligence” must not be allowed to act alone on major military actions. He presents the agreement as one of the major successes of Donald Trump's Asian tour [1].

On the Chinese side, the official readout states that Xi Jinping called on the two countries to strengthen communication on AI-related security risks and to ensure that AI remains “under human control” [3].
But neither government has published a text specifying which systems are covered, what “human control” means or how to verify it [3].
Scott Bessent insists that this agreement is separate from the race for AI supremacy. US labs must keep their lead over “dangerous” Chinese models, which he says are used for cyberattacks [3].

In Geneva, according to Reuters on Saturday, November 21, states agreed to open negotiations at the UN to regulate “killer robots,” or autonomous weapons, by 2028, but Russia's opposition weakened the outcome [4].
The Shenzhen summit also produced a pledge by Trump, Xi and Putin to open talks on nuclear risks [5].
Key takeaway: Washington and Beijing assert at leader level that a machine must not decide alone on a major military action, but for now it is a statement of intent, with no written rule.

It is a change of tone for Beijing. In 2024, a non-binding international declaration known as REAIM already called for maintaining human control over the use of nuclear weapons, and China had not signed it [3]. The understanding announced in Shenzhen is therefore notable, even if it remains bilateral.

The limits are clear: no list of the weapons covered, no definition, no verification mechanism [3]. And the rivalry continues: Washington wants to keep its technological lead and accuses Chinese models of being used for cyberattacks [3].

Globally, regulation is advancing slowly: in Geneva, negotiations on autonomous weapons aim for an agreement within two years, and Russia has applied the brakes [4]. An agreement between Washington and Beijing could weigh on these talks, since they are the two countries developing military AI the most.

AI is making its way into defense: drones, target detection, intelligence analysis. The question is simple: who presses the button? What Washington and Beijing are promising is that it will always be a human for major decisions. Until there is a signed, verifiable text, take this announcement as a first step, not a guarantee.

United States
United States: consumer sentiment rebounds after the elections, but a Fed official says rates are still too low with inflation at 3.8%

The University of Michigan consumer sentiment index rose to 51.5 in November from 48 in October, lifted by the elections and cheaper gasoline. The same day, Fed Governor Lisa Cook argued in Santiago, Chile, for further rate hikes [1][3].
The final November index stands at 51.5, compared with 48.0 in October and 51.0 in November 2025; the preliminary estimate, taken before the vote, was 51 [1][2].
Joanne Hsu, the survey's director, speaks of a “significant move, but the level remains relatively low”: sentiment is still 9% below February, before the conflict with Iran began [1].
Lower-income households were relieved by cheaper gasoline, while large stockholders were worried by AI-related market jolts; the survey covers the period from October 20 to November 16 [1].
Consumers still cite inflation, far more than unemployment, as their main source of hardship [6].

On Friday, November 20, at a Central Bank of Chile conference in Santiago, Lisa Cook estimated that consumer prices (PCE index) rose 3.8% year on year in October, and 3.2% excluding energy and food [3].

Inflation has exceeded the Fed's 2% target for 67 months [3], “nearly six years,” according to the official text of the speech [4]. According to Lisa Cook, the current rate is not high enough: if the Fed falls behind, “additional and larger increases may be needed later to catch up” [3][5].
Lisa Cook was one of two officials who opposed holding the policy rate between 3.75% and 4% last month [3].
Key takeaway: the US economy is holding up, but inflation remains nearly twice the target, and the Fed is preparing to raise rates just as households are barely starting to regain confidence [1][3].

Lisa Cook considers growth “strong and accelerating” and the labor market “solid,” but warns: “Wages are rising, but not enough to offset the harmful effects of inflation” [3]. That is the whole dilemma: a well-functioning economy leaves room for higher rates, but those hikes make household credit more expensive.

An index of 51.5 remains historically very low, and Joanne Hsu sees it mainly as the effect of the elections and cheaper gasoline [1]. If the Fed raises rates in December, mortgage lending and consumer spending could slow again.

The disagreement within the Fed is therefore out in the open: last month, the majority chose to wait, while Lisa Cook and another official already wanted to raise rates [3]. Her public warnings, from a forum of central bankers, show that the camp favoring a rapid hike is gaining ground [3][5].

When the Fed raises rates, the dollar often strengthens: your trips to the United States cost more in euros, but European companies that sell there benefit. And the ECB watches closely what Washington does.

Ukraine: Zelensky calls Putin a “killer” after Trump called him his “friend,” and demands security guarantees “forever”

On Saturday, November 21, Volodymyr Zelensky called Vladimir Putin a “killer,” a few days after Donald Trump referred to the Russian leader as his “friend.” The Ukrainian president is demanding security guarantees that outlast Trump's term, as Russia fired another 148 drones overnight [1][2][3].
Volodymyr Zelensky said Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin both wanted to end the war but “did not know how,” and called the Russian president a “killer” [1].

His remarks follow a massive Russian strike: according to him, more than 400 attack drones and more than 110 missiles were fired [1]. The wave killed at least seven people in Kyiv and damaged bridges over the Dnipro [6].

Overnight from November 20 to 21, Russia launched another three ballistic missiles and 148 drones, including 87 jet-powered drones, according to the Ukrainian Air Force as cited by the Kyiv Independent [3].
In a post on X on November 21, Volodymyr Zelensky called for security guarantees valid beyond Donald Trump's term, “not for two years, but forever” [2].
He returns to the meeting of the “coalition of the willing” held in Berlin on November 19, and defends NATO membership as “the clearest security guarantee for Ukraine” [2].
US envoy Jared Kushner said Donald Trump was open to “NATO-style” guarantees, but Volodymyr Zelensky says he has not yet seen written commitments [3].
In Berlin, Greek Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis called for a ceasefire, a moratorium on strikes against energy infrastructure and a naval ceasefire in the Black Sea [4].
Key takeaway: at the heart of the peace negotiations, Kyiv does not want promises that would disappear when Donald Trump leaves the White House [2].

Security guarantees are commitments by third countries to defend Ukraine if Russia attacked again. The whole question is how solid they are: a simple political declaration can be forgotten, while a treaty or NATO membership is far more binding [2][3].

The choice of words matters: by calling Putin a “killer” just after Trump called him his “friend,” Zelensky distances himself from Washington without breaking with the US envoys, from whom he expects written commitments [1][3].
On the ground, the overnight strikes continue despite the diplomacy, targeting bridges, energy and cities ahead of winter [1][3][6].

The shape peace takes in Ukraine will determine the level of European military spending, and thus part of your taxes, as well as energy prices. A fragile peace, without solid guarantees, would leave the risk of a new war hanging.

After nearly nine years of talks, China opens its services and screens to South Korea: Korean films and video games get better treatment, but not K-pop

China and South Korea have wrapped up the second phase of their free trade agreement, covering services, investment and finance. Announced by Beijing on November 18 and welcomed by Lee Jae-myung and Xi Jinping in Shenzhen, it still has to be signed, with no date set [1][4][5].
China's Ministry of Commerce announced on November 18 the “substantial conclusion” of the second phase of negotiations on the China-South Korea free trade agreement [1].
South Korean President Lee Jae-myung and Xi Jinping welcomed this progress at their meeting in Shenzhen, on the sidelines of the APEC summit [5].
The text modernizes four chapters of the original agreement: investment, trade in services, financial services and economic cooperation [1].
The two countries are switching to a “negative list” for investment, services and finance: everything is open except what is explicitly excluded [4].
South Korean films and online games will receive “most-favored-nation” treatment, meaning no worse than those of any other country [3].
However, large public performances, such as K-pop concerts, remain entirely outside the agreement [3].

Negotiations began in March 2018 [2]. Technical details, translations and legal review still have to be finalized before signing; no timetable has been given and the full text will only be published afterward [4].
Key takeaway: South Korea gains better access to the Chinese market for its services, its investments and part of its culture, after years of negotiations.
This second phase covers the sectors that matter most for a modern economy: banking, insurance, business services, investment in factories, and culture [1].

The switch to a “negative list” is the real novelty: instead of listing the sectors that are open, it lists those that remain closed, which is in principle more favorable to foreign companies [4]. But in Korea, the business press remains cautious: the Seoul Economic Daily says the agreement must deliver “real market opening” [6].

On the Chinese side, state media highlight the expected benefits for travel between the two countries [7]. The exclusion of K-pop concerts shows that culture remains a sensitive subject for Beijing [3].

Korean series, films and games have become a heavyweight of the global cultural economy. Seeing China open its door to them a little wider is a sign of easing tensions between two neighbors that trade enormously. For Europe, it is also a reminder: China is signing deals with its neighbors while relations with Washington remain tense.

Montenegro
Montenegro: 25 of 33 chapters closed with the EU, Podgorica aims to finish negotiations by December

On Thursday, November 19, in Brussels, Montenegro provisionally closed two more chapters of its European Union accession negotiations: taxation and regional policy. It has now closed 25 out of 33 and wants to finish everything by the end of 2026, which would make it the EU's next member [1][2][3].
The 31st accession conference with Montenegro, held at the Council of the EU, closed chapter 16 (taxation) and chapter 22 (regional policy and coordination of structural instruments) [1][2].

Nine of the 25 closed chapters were closed under the Irish presidency of the Council of the EU, which runs this half-year [4]. Agence Europe notes that more than 75% of the chapters are now provisionally closed [4].
European Affairs Minister Maida Gorčević speaks of “25 out of 35,” as the negotiating framework provides for two additional chapters [3].

Eight chapters remain: financial services, transport, energy, judiciary and fundamental rights, justice and security, environment and climate, foreign policy, and financial and budgetary provisions [2][3].
Enlargement Commissioner Marta Kos believes an accession treaty could be signed as early as June 2027, for entry as the 28th member in 2028 [5][6].
The main obstacle is Croatia, which is setting bilateral conditions. “We need Croatia and Montenegro to find solutions to their disputes,” Marta Kos warned [5].
Key takeaway: Montenegro is the most advanced candidate in the Balkans, and each closed chapter brings it closer to joining the EU in 2028 as the 28th member [5][6].

Closing a chapter means the EU considers Montenegrin law aligned with its own in that area. Chapter 22 matters for the economy: it prepares the country to receive and manage European regional funds, which finance roads, water networks and renovations [1][2].

The remaining chapters are the hardest politically, especially the judiciary and fundamental rights. And the EU's internal politics are becoming the main obstacle: bilateral demands from a member state such as Croatia can slow what comes next [5][8].

For the other candidates, the contrast is stark: Albania aims to finish its negotiations by the end of 2027, while North Macedonia has not opened any cluster of chapters, blocked by Bulgaria, which demands that it recognize its Bulgarian minority in its Constitution [7]. Its president, Gordana Siljanovska-Davkova, says her country's accession is being “held hostage” [7].

If it joins, traveling, working or investing there will become as simple as in any other member state. It is also a test: can the EU still enlarge, as the war in Ukraine revives the debate on enlargement?

news.2026-11-22-malawi-penurie-carburant: Lilongwe, Malawi
Malawi
Malawi: still no date for fuel to return, as the country runs short of dollars and refuses to devalue despite the IMF

A year after Peter Mutharika's return to power, Malawi remains paralyzed by a fuel shortage. The government cannot say when deliveries will resume. The cause: a lack of dollars to pay for imports, while the country refuses the devaluation the IMF demands before lending to it again [1][4][5].
On November 17, government spokesman Shadric Namalomba gave no date for the fuel's arrival, promising only a “marked improvement in the coming days” [1].

President Peter Mutharika blames logistics: “The fuel is there. We have it in all the ports, in Tanzania, in Nacala, Beira, Tanga and Dar es Salaam” [2]. The number of road haulers has fallen from about 850 in 2020 to 350-380 today, according to their association [3].
In October, the shortage had already become a national emergency, with motorists queuing for days [6].
The central bank sold 590 kilograms of gold to raise $78 million. Yet the state fuel company (NOCMA) estimates its needs at about $49 million in foreign currency per month [4][7].
The kwacha officially trades at around 1,750 to the dollar, but between 3,500 and 5,000 on the parallel market [4].
Malawi has had no IMF loan since May 2025. A Fund mission from June 9 to 18, 2026, left without an agreement: the IMF wants a freer kwacha, while the government promises not to devalue [5].
The IMF forecasts about 2.2% growth and 24.4% inflation for 2026 [4].
Key takeaway: Malawi has kwachas but no dollars. Without foreign currency, it cannot pay for imported fuel, and the whole economy slows down [4].

The mechanism: by setting an official rate two to three times more favorable than the street rate, the state makes dollars scarce in banks. Importers cannot get them at the counter, deliveries stop, and a black market thrives [4][5].

The IMF makes its aid conditional on a more flexible exchange rate. Devaluing would bring in dollars but would sharply raise the price of imported goods, in a country where inflation already exceeds 24% [4][5]. The Fund nevertheless welcomes the fuel and sugar pricing reforms [4].

The gold sale covers only a little more than a month and a half of fuel needs [4][7]. Peter Mutharika, who returned in early November after nearly a month in South Africa, is expected to deliver lasting solutions [8].

When a country sets its exchange rate too far from reality, it often ends in lines at the pump. Malawi shows the dilemma: devaluing hurts right away (higher prices), not devaluing hurts for longer (shortages).

Trinidad and Tobago sends a team to Caracas to secure a deal on Venezuelan gas by the end of November

A technical team from Trinidad and Tobago is due to meet Venezuela's Hydrocarbons Ministry in Caracas early in the week. The goal: to conclude by the end of November an agreement to develop shared offshore gas fields, including the Dragon field [1][2].
A high-level meeting is due to follow a few days later, with Energy Minister Roodal Moonilal and Minister of Foreign and Caricom Affairs Sean Sobers [1].
The targeted fields are Dragon and Loran-Manatee, off Trinidad, in waters linked to Venezuela [3]. BNamericas mentions an agreement covering 1.7 Tcf (trillion cubic feet) of gas [2].
On October 30, Roodal Moonilal told Parliament that a gas measurement agreement was close to being signed [4].
Development also requires a separate green light from the United States, and it is unclear whether Caracas accepts the end-of-November deadline [3].
Key takeaway: Trinidad and Tobago, a major Caribbean gas producer, is seeking a new source just across its maritime border with Venezuela [2][3].

The file depends on Washington, which governs any project with Venezuela through its sanctions. Kamla Persad-Bissessar's government is reviving it after the US midterm elections [3]. In a sign of the strain on gas, she also warned that her country would not subsidize electricity or gas for future AI sites in Jamaica [5].
Gas is also used to make fertilizers and plastics. A deal would strengthen regional supply, but everything depends on the US green light.

news.2026-11-22-bresil-lula-paquet-fisca: Brazil: “The financial system will not teach me how to run the country,” Lula says in defense of his savings plan

On Saturday, November 21, during an online livestream with congressman André Janones, Lula defended the fiscal package presented this month, said it did not affect small businesses and denied any increase in the minimum retirement age [1][2].
“The financial system will not teach me how to run the country,” the Brazilian president said, also criticizing the reaction of part of the left to his plan [1].
